passage: My name is Tanuja. When I was ten, I played the mango seller in our school play. On the day, I walked on with my basket and said my first line, and someone in the front row laughed. I didn't expect it and forgot my second line for a second. I looked at Zeenat, our teacher, at the side of the stage. She mouthed the word and I said it louder than before. More people laughed and I noticed that the ones at the back were leaning forward. Later, when I said the sad line, they went completely silent. I couldn't tell if that was good or bad, but Zeenat said silence can mean they were listening.

qa.q: What role did Tanuja play in the school play?
qa.a: Tanuja played the mango seller.

qa.q: What did Tanuja think when the audience went silent during the sad line?
qa.a: Tanuja couldn't tell whether the silence was good or bad. Zeenat's remark suggests it could mean they were listening rather than bored.

qa.q: What could Tanuja try next time when she forgets a line?
qa.a: Tanuja could look at Zeenat at the side for the cue, take a breath, and keep going, as Tanuja did.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see the silence in the audience?
qa.a: Zeenat sees silence as a sign that people were paying attention, and helps Tanuja read it as engagement instead of a judgment.

grounding: A performing child notices laughter and silence, learns to adjust, and understands reactions as cues about engagement.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 6 play rehearsal. Ankita was the narrator in this afternoon's run-through for the parents' evening. In the first scene the audience of Class 3 children laughed at her funny voice, and she seemed to enjoy it and slowed down. In the second scene, some children began fidgeting and one yawned. I noticed Ankita's eyes flick to them and her voice speed up, then drop. I coached her after: "What did you see from the stage?" She said, "They got bored." I asked what she could try, and she suggested adding a pause and a louder line. We tried it. I will remind her that fidgeting tells us about the scene, not about her worth. Francis (stage manager) will time the next run. 🙂

qa.q: What role did Ankita have in the play?
qa.a: She was the narrator.

qa.q: What was Ankita likely thinking when she saw the children fidgeting and yawning, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: She likely thought they were bored, and her speeding up shows she was worried. The fidgeting might also come from the second scene being long or the children being tired.

qa.q: What could Ankita try when she notices restless children in the audience?
qa.a: She could add a pause, use a louder or livelier line, and adjust the pace, as she and the teacher tried after rehearsal.

qa.q: How might Francis help with the next run?
qa.a: As stage manager Francis will time the run, which gives Ankita information about the pace so she can adjust without taking the reaction as a verdict on herself.

grounding: A performing child notices laughter and fidgeting, adjusts, and is reminded that audience reactions are cues, not a verdict on worth.

passage:
Wednesday
School play today! I was the lion in the jungle story. When I roared the first time, the little kids in the front row laughed. I got a fright because it was supposed to be scary. My face went hot and I almost forgot my line.
But then I saw that they were laughing because it was a good roar, not because I was bad. So on the second roar I made it even bigger and shook my mane. Everyone laughed again and one boy clapped. Jatin, who was the monkey, winked at me from the tree.
At the end Ma'am said the audience loved the lion. I'm going to be a funny lion forever now.
- Simran

qa.q: What part did Simran play?
qa.a: The lion in the jungle story.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when the front row first laughed?
qa.a: Simran felt startled and embarrassed, worried the laugh meant the roar was bad.

qa.q: What did Simran do after reading the audience's laughter?
qa.a: Simran made the second roar even bigger and shook the mane, using the laughter as a sign the audience was enjoying it.

qa.q: How might Jatin have seen the scene from the tree?
qa.a: Jatin probably enjoyed seeing Simran adapt and gave a wink to show support.

grounding: A child in a school play notices audience laughter, adjusts, and learns it shows engagement, not a verdict on worth.

passage:
At the village Ramlila, Arnab played Lakshman. During his long speech to Ram, he noticed people shifting, a baby crying, and two men near the tea stall talking loudly.
His throat tightened. Were they bored of him?
Then he remembered what Mohit Bhaiya said in practice: "When they fidget, give them something to watch."
Arnab stepped forward, raised his bow high, and paused. The talking stopped. He finished the speech louder and slower. Some children in front sat up straight.
Afterward Mohit clapped his shoulder. "You saw them, and you fixed it."
Arnab grinned, but he said, "It was a long speech, na? Maybe they were just tired."

qa.q: What did Arnab do with his bow during the speech?
qa.a: He raised his bow high and paused.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he noticed people fidgeting?
qa.a: He felt nervous and worried that the audience was bored of him.

qa.q: What small step helped Arnab regain attention?
qa.a: He added a strong gesture and a pause, giving the audience something to watch.

qa.q: Why might the audience have fidgeted even if Arnab was good?
qa.a: It was a long speech and people may have been tired, so fidgeting was about engagement, not his worth.

grounding: A child performing in a village Ramlila notices fidgeting, adjusts his performance, and realises it isn't a judgment of him.

passage:
In the school play in Toronto, Jin had the funniest line: "My sock is alive!" At rehearsal it always got a big laugh. But on the night, silence. Jin's stomach dropped. Maybe she was terrible.
Backstage, Santiago whispered, "They were listening! Look, the grandpa in the front row is still smiling."
Jin peeked through the curtain. People were leaning forward, waiting.
In the next scene she slowed down, let the funny pause stretch, and the whole hall laughed. After the play, a small girl ran up to her. "The sock was my favourite!"
Jin laughed. Maybe silence doesn't mean they don't like you.

qa.q: What was Jin's funniest line?
qa.a: "My sock is alive!"

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when her line got silence?
qa.a: Jin felt anxious and disappointed, worrying she was terrible.

qa.q: What advice did Santiago give that helped Jin?
qa.a: Santiago pointed out that the audience was listening and smiling, which helped Jin see silence as engagement.

qa.q: How might the small girl in the audience have felt about Jin's performance?
qa.a: She was delighted and loved the sock line, showing Jin's acting had reached her.

grounding: A child in a school play reads silence, adjusts timing, and learns audience reactions are cues about engagement.

passage: In the school hall the fans were switched off for the microphones, and the air was thick. Rekha, playing the forgetful king, reached her long speech about lost keys. Halfway through, she saw the front row squirming: a boy yawning, two girls whispering. Her stomach dipped. Were they bored of her? She took a breath, stepped closer to the edge, and patted each pocket slowly as she spoke. A small laugh came. She patted her crown too. A bigger laugh. Backstage, Nirmala Ma'am handed her water. "You read them beautifully." "But they were yawning at first," Rekha said. "It's hot, and that speech is long. The yawns were about the room, not about you."

qa.q: What part was Rekha playing?
qa.a: The forgetful king.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when her stomach dipped?
qa.a: She felt anxious and a little hurt, wondering if the audience was bored of her personally.

qa.q: Which adjustment worked, and why?
qa.a: Stepping closer and adding slow pocket-patting, then the crown, gave the restless audience something to watch, and it won laughs 😊

qa.q: How might the front row have experienced the scene?
qa.a: The front row was hot and restless through a long speech, then perked up and laughed at the new pocket-patting.

grounding: It shows a child in a school play noticing fidgeting and laughter, adjusting the performance, and learning the cues were about engagement, not her worth.
